verses.text: There was a man named Elkanah from Ramathaim Zophim in Ephraim's hill country. He was an Ephraimite, the son of Jeroham, son of Elihu, son of Tohu, son of Zuph.
He had two wives, Hannah and Peninnah. Peninnah had children, but Hannah had none.
Every year Elkanah left his town to worship and offer sacrifices to the LORD of Armies at Shiloh. Eli's two sons, Hophni and Phinehas, served there as priests to the LORD.
On the day Elkanah offered his sacrifice, he gave portions to Peninnah and all her sons and daughters.
He gave Hannah a double portion because he loved her, though the LORD had kept her from having children.
Her rival tormented her to upset her because the LORD had kept her from having children.
This went on year after year whenever Hannah went up to the LORD's house. Peninnah would taunt her until Hannah cried and wouldn't eat.
Her husband Elkanah asked her, “Hannah, why are you crying? Why won't you eat? Why are you grieving? Don't I mean more to you than ten sons?”
After they finished eating and drinking at Shiloh, Hannah got up. Eli the priest was sitting in his seat by the doorpost of the LORD's temple.
Hannah was in deep anguish. She prayed to the LORD and wept bitterly.

She made a vow: “LORD of Armies, if you look at your servant's suffering, remember me and don't forget me, and give me a son, I'll give him to you for his whole life. No razor will ever touch his head.”
As she kept praying before the LORD, Eli watched her mouth.
Hannah was praying in her heart. Her lips moved, but her voice couldn't be heard. Eli thought she was drunk.
He asked her, “How long are you going to stay drunk? Put the wine away.”
Hannah answered, “No, sir. I'm a woman in deep distress. I haven't had any wine or strong drink. I've been pouring out my heart before the LORD.
Please don't think I'm a wicked woman. I've been speaking out of all my pain and grief.”
Eli answered, “Go in peace. May the God of Israel give you what you've asked him for.”
She said, “May I find favor with you.” Then she went her way and ate, and her face was no longer sad.
They got up early the next morning and worshiped the LORD. Then they went back home to Ramah. Elkanah slept with his wife Hannah, and the LORD remembered her.
In time Hannah became pregnant and gave birth to a son. She named him Samuel, saying, “I asked the LORD for him.”
Elkanah and his whole household went up to bring the yearly sacrifice to the LORD and fulfill his vow.
Hannah stayed behind. She told her husband, “Once the boy is weaned, I'll take him to appear before the LORD and stay there for good.”
Elkanah told her, “Do what seems best to you. Stay here until you've weaned him. May the LORD make his word stand.” So Hannah stayed and nursed her son until he was weaned.
When she'd weaned him, she took him to the LORD's house at Shiloh, bringing three bulls, an ephah of flour, and a container of wine. The boy was still young.
They slaughtered the bull and brought the boy to Eli.
Hannah said, “Pardon me, sir. As surely as you live, I'm the woman who stood here beside you praying to the LORD.
I prayed for this child, and the LORD gave me what I asked him for.
Now I'm giving him to the LORD. He belongs to the LORD for as long as he lives.” And he worshiped the LORD there.
Hannah prayed, “My heart celebrates in the LORD! The LORD has lifted my horn in triumph. I can speak boldly over my enemies because I rejoice in how you've rescued me.
Nobody is holy like the LORD. There is no one besides you, and no rock like our God.
Stop talking so proudly. Don't let arrogance come out of your mouth. The LORD knows everything, and he weighs what people do.
The bows of the mighty are broken, and those who stumbled are clothed with strength.

People who had plenty now work for a piece of bread, while those who went hungry have enough. The woman who couldn't have children has given birth to seven, while the woman with many children is wasting away.
The LORD takes life and gives life. He brings people down to Sheol and raises them up.
The LORD makes people poor or rich. He brings people low, and he lifts them up.

He raises the poor from the dust and lifts the needy from the garbage heap. He seats them with princes and gives them a place of honor. The pillars of the earth belong to the LORD. He set the world on them.
He'll guard the steps of his faithful ones, but the wicked will be silenced in darkness. Nobody wins by strength alone.

Those who fight the LORD will be shattered. He'll thunder against them from heaven. The LORD will judge to the ends of the earth. He'll give strength to his king and raise up the horn of his anointed one.”
Elkanah went home to Ramah, but the boy stayed and served the LORD under Eli the priest.
Eli's sons were wicked men who didn't know the LORD.
Here's how the priests treated people. Whenever someone brought a sacrifice, the priest's servant arrived while the meat was boiling, carrying a three-pronged fork.
He stuck the fork into the pan, kettle, cauldron, or pot, and the priest kept whatever came up on it. They did this to every Israelite who came to Shiloh.
Even before the fat was burned, the priest's servant would tell the person offering the sacrifice, “Give the priest meat to roast. He wants it raw. He won't take boiled meat.”
If the person said, “Burn the fat first, and then take as much as you want,” the servant would answer, “Give it to me now, or I'll take it by force.”
The young men's sin was very serious in the LORD's sight because they treated his offering with contempt.
Meanwhile Samuel served before the LORD. He was still a boy and wore a linen ephod.
Each year his mother made him a little robe and brought it when she came with her husband to offer the yearly sacrifice.
Eli would bless Elkanah and his wife, saying, “May the LORD give you children through this woman in place of the child she asked for and gave to the LORD.” Then they went home.
The LORD cared for Hannah. She became pregnant and had three sons and two daughters. Samuel grew up in the LORD's presence.
By then Eli was very old. He heard how his sons were treating all Israel and how they slept with the women who served at the entrance to the Tent of Meeting.
He asked them, “Why are you doing these things? I'm hearing about your evil behavior from everyone.
This has to stop, my sons. What I'm hearing is terrible. You're leading the LORD's people into disobedience.

If someone sins against another person, God can judge between them. But if someone sins against the LORD, who can plead for them?” They didn't listen to their father, because the LORD intended to put them to death.
Samuel kept growing and found more favor with both the LORD and the people.
A man of God came to Eli and said, “The LORD says, ‘Didn't I reveal myself to your ancestor's family when they were enslaved by Pharaoh in Egypt?

Didn't I choose your ancestor from all of Israel's tribes to be my priest, to go up to my altar, burn incense, and wear an ephod before me? Didn't I give his household all the Israelites' offerings made by fire?

Why do you treat the sacrifices and offerings I commanded for my dwelling with contempt? Why do you honor your sons above me and fatten yourselves on the best of every offering from my people Israel?’

So the LORD, the God of Israel, says, ‘I did promise that your family and your ancestor's family would serve before me forever.’ But now the LORD says, ‘Far be that from me. I'll honor those who honor me, and those who despise me will be cursed.
The time is coming when I'll cut short your strength and the strength of your ancestral family, so no man in your household will live to old age.
You'll see trouble in my dwelling, even while I give Israel good things in abundance. There will never be an old man in your household.
Anyone I leave serving at my altar will wear out your eyes with tears and bring grief to your heart. Your descendants will die in the prime of their lives.
What happens to your sons Hophni and Phinehas will be your sign. They'll both die on the same day.
I'll raise up a faithful priest who will do what's in my heart and mind. I'll give him a family that endures, and he'll serve before my anointed one forever.
Everyone left in your household will come and bow before him for a piece of silver and a loaf of bread. They'll say, “Please give me one of the priests' duties so I can have a bite to eat.”’”
The boy Samuel served the LORD under Eli. In those days messages from the LORD were rare, and visions didn't happen often.
One night Eli had gone to lie down in his usual place. His eyesight had grown so dim he could barely see.
God's lamp was still burning, and Samuel had lain down in the LORD's temple, where God's ark was kept.
The LORD called Samuel, and Samuel answered, “Here I am.”
He ran to Eli and said, “Here I am. You called me.” Eli said, “I didn't call you. Go lie down again.” So Samuel went back to bed.
The LORD called again, “Samuel!” Samuel got up and went to Eli. “Here I am. You called me.” Eli answered, “I didn't call you, my son. Go lie down again.”
Samuel didn't yet know the LORD, because the LORD hadn't revealed his word to him yet.
The LORD called Samuel a third time. He got up and went to Eli. “Here I am. You called me.” Then Eli realized it was the LORD calling the boy.
Eli told Samuel, “Go lie down. If he calls you again, say, ‘Speak, LORD. Your servant is listening.’” So Samuel went back and lay down in his place.
The LORD came and stood there, calling out as before, “Samuel! Samuel!” Samuel answered, “Speak. Your servant is listening.”
The LORD told Samuel, “I'm about to do something in Israel that will make the ears of everyone who hears about it ring.
That day I'll carry out everything I said against Eli and his household, from beginning to end.
I told him I'd judge his family forever for the wrong he knew about. His sons brought a curse on themselves, and he did nothing to stop them.
That's why I swore to Eli's household that no sacrifice or offering would ever take away the guilt of his family.”
Samuel stayed in bed until morning, then opened the doors of the LORD's house. He was afraid to tell Eli about the vision.
Eli called him, “Samuel, my son!” He answered, “Here I am.”
Eli asked, “What did he say to you? Please don't hide it from me. May God deal with you severely if you hide anything he told you.”
So Samuel told him everything and held nothing back. Eli said, “He is the LORD. Let him do what seems good to him.”
Samuel grew up, and the LORD was with him. He let none of Samuel's words fall to the ground.
All Israel, from Dan to Beersheba, knew that Samuel had been established as a prophet of the LORD.
The LORD continued to appear at Shiloh, where he revealed himself to Samuel through his word.
Samuel's word reached all Israel. Israel went out to fight the Philistines and camped near Ebenezer, while the Philistines camped at Aphek.
The Philistines lined up against Israel. When the fighting began, they defeated Israel and killed about four thousand men on the battlefield.

When the troops returned to camp, Israel's elders asked, “Why did the LORD let the Philistines defeat us today? Let's bring the ark of the LORD's covenant from Shiloh. If it's here among us, it can save us from our enemies.”
So they sent to Shiloh and brought back the ark of the covenant of the LORD of Armies, who sits enthroned above the cherubim. Eli's sons Hophni and Phinehas were there with God's ark of the covenant.
When the ark of the LORD's covenant entered the camp, all Israel shouted so loudly the ground shook.
The Philistines heard the roar and asked, “What does all that shouting in the Hebrews' camp mean?” Then they found out the LORD's ark had come into the camp.
They were afraid and said, “God has come into their camp. We're in trouble! Nothing like this has ever happened before.
We're doomed! Who can save us from these mighty gods? These are the gods that struck the Egyptians with every kind of plague in the wilderness.
Be strong, Philistines! Fight like men, or you'll become slaves to the Hebrews just as they've been slaves to you. Stand your ground and fight!”
The Philistines fought and defeated Israel, and each man fled to his own tent. It was a terrible slaughter. Thirty thousand Israelite foot soldiers fell.
God's ark was captured, and Eli's two sons, Hophni and Phinehas, were killed.
That same day a man from Benjamin ran from the battle to Shiloh with his clothes torn and dirt on his head.
When he arrived, Eli was sitting by the road watching, worried sick about God's ark. When the man reached town and told what had happened, the whole town cried out.
Eli heard the uproar and asked, “What is all that noise?” The man hurried over to tell him.
Eli was ninety-eight years old. His eyes stared straight ahead, and he couldn't see.
The man said, “I've come from the army. I ran from the battlefield today.” Eli asked, “What happened, my son?”
The messenger answered, “Israel ran from the Philistines, and many of our people were killed. Your two sons, Hophni and Phinehas, are dead too, and God's ark has been captured.”
At the mention of God's ark, Eli fell backward off his seat beside the gate. He was old and heavy, and the fall broke his neck and killed him. He had judged Israel forty years.

His daughter-in-law, Phinehas's wife, was pregnant and close to giving birth. When she heard that God's ark had been captured and that her husband and father-in-law were dead, she doubled over as labor came on and gave birth.
As she was dying, the women standing beside her said, “Don't be afraid. You've had a son.” She didn't answer or pay attention.
She named the boy Ichabod, saying, “The glory has left Israel!” She said this because God's ark was captured and her husband and father-in-law were dead.
She said, “The glory has left Israel because God's ark has been captured.”
After capturing God's ark, the Philistines took it from Ebenezer to Ashdod.
They carried it into Dagon's temple and set it beside Dagon.
Early the next morning the people of Ashdod found Dagon lying facedown on the ground in front of the LORD's ark. They lifted him up and put him back in place.
When they got up early the next morning, Dagon had fallen facedown again before the LORD's ark. His head and both hands lay cut off on the threshold. Only his torso was intact.
That's why to this day Dagon's priests and everyone who enters his temple in Ashdod avoid stepping on the threshold.
The LORD's hand weighed heavily on the people of Ashdod. He devastated the town and the surrounding area and struck the people with tumors.
When the people saw what was happening, they said, “The ark of Israel's God can't stay here. His hand is heavy on us and on Dagon our god.”
So they called all the Philistine rulers together and asked, “What should we do with the ark of Israel's God?” The rulers said to move it to Gath, and that's where they took it.
After they brought it there, the LORD's hand came against the city and threw it into panic. He struck the people, young and old alike, and tumors broke out on them.
They sent God's ark to Ekron. As it arrived, the people of Ekron cried out, “They've brought the ark of Israel's God here to kill us and our people!”

They called the Philistine rulers together and said, “Send the ark of Israel's God back where it belongs, before it kills us and our people.” Deadly panic had spread through the city, and God's hand weighed heavily on it.
Those who survived were struck with tumors, and the city's cries rose to heaven.
The LORD's ark stayed in Philistine territory for seven months.
The Philistines called their priests and diviners and asked, “What should we do with the LORD's ark? Tell us how to send it back where it belongs.”

They answered, “If you send back the ark of Israel's God, don't send it back empty. Be sure to send a guilt offering with it. Then you'll be healed, and you'll know why his hand hasn't lifted from you.”

They asked, “What guilt offering should we send him?” The priests and diviners answered, “Five gold tumors and five gold mice, one for each Philistine ruler, because the same plague struck you and your rulers.
Make models of the tumors and of the mice ravaging your land, and give glory to Israel's God. Maybe he'll lift his hand from you, your gods, and your land.
Why harden your hearts the way Pharaoh and the Egyptians did? Once God did wonders among them, didn't they let the people leave?
Now get a new cart ready and take two nursing cows that have never worn a yoke. Hitch them to the cart and shut their calves up at home, away from them.
Put the LORD's ark on the cart. Put the gold objects you're sending as a guilt offering in a box beside it. Then send the cart on its way.
Watch where it goes. If it heads toward its own territory at Beth Shemesh, Israel's God brought this disaster on us. If it doesn't, we'll know his hand didn't strike us and it happened by chance.”
The men did as they were told. They hitched two nursing cows to the cart and shut their calves up at home.
They put the LORD's ark on the cart with the box holding the gold mice and the gold models of their tumors.
The cows went straight along the road to Beth Shemesh, lowing as they went. They didn't turn right or left. The Philistine rulers followed them as far as the border of Beth Shemesh.
The people of Beth Shemesh were harvesting wheat in the valley. When they looked up and saw the ark, they were overjoyed.
The cart rolled into the field of Joshua of Beth Shemesh and stopped beside a large stone. The people split up the cart for wood and offered the cows as a burnt offering to the LORD.
The Levites took down the LORD's ark and the box with the gold objects and set them on the large stone. That day the people of Beth Shemesh brought burnt offerings and other sacrifices to the LORD.
The five Philistine rulers saw what happened and went back to Ekron that same day.
The gold tumors the Philistines sent as a guilt offering to the LORD were one each for Ashdod, Gaza, Ashkelon, Gath, and Ekron.

The gold mice represented all the Philistine towns ruled by the five leaders, whether fortified towns or country villages, as far as the large stone where they set the LORD's ark. That stone is still in the field of Joshua of Beth Shemesh today.
The LORD struck down fifty thousand and seventy men of Beth Shemesh because they had looked inside the LORD's ark. The people mourned because the LORD had struck them with such a great slaughter.
The people of Beth Shemesh asked, “Who can stand before the LORD, this holy God? Where can the ark go from here?”
They sent messengers to Kiriath Jearim to say, “The Philistines have returned the LORD's ark. Come down and take it up to your town.”
The men of Kiriath Jearim came for the LORD's ark and brought it to Abinadab's house on the hill. They set apart his son Eleazar to look after it.
The ark stayed in Kiriath Jearim a long time, twenty years in all. The whole house of Israel mourned and longed for the LORD.

Samuel told all Israel, “If you're coming back to the LORD with your whole heart, get rid of the foreign gods and the Ashtaroth. Turn your hearts toward the LORD and serve him alone, and he'll rescue you from the Philistines.”
So the Israelites got rid of the Baals and the Ashtaroth and served only the LORD.
Samuel said, “Gather all Israel at Mizpah, and I'll pray to the LORD for you.”
They gathered at Mizpah, drew water, and poured it out before the LORD. They fasted that day and said, “We've sinned against the LORD.” Samuel judged the Israelites at Mizpah.
When the Philistine rulers heard that the Israelites had gathered at Mizpah, they went up against them. The Israelites heard they were coming and were afraid.
They told Samuel, “Keep crying out to the LORD our God for us. Ask him to rescue us from the Philistines.”
Samuel took a nursing lamb and offered it whole to the LORD as a burnt offering. He cried out to the LORD for Israel, and the LORD answered.
As Samuel was offering the sacrifice, the Philistines came near to fight. The LORD thundered against them so loudly that they were thrown into confusion and defeated before Israel.
The Israelites rushed out from Mizpah and pursued the Philistines, striking them down as far as the area below Beth Kar.
Samuel took a stone, set it up between Mizpah and Shen, and named it Ebenezer. He said, “The LORD has helped us this far.”
The Philistines were subdued and stopped crossing into Israel's territory. The LORD's hand was against them throughout Samuel's life.
Israel got back the towns the Philistines had taken, from Ekron to Gath, and recovered the surrounding territory. There was also peace between Israel and the Amorites.
Samuel judged Israel for the rest of his life.
Every year he traveled a circuit through Bethel, Gilgal, and Mizpah, judging Israel at each place.
Then he returned home to Ramah, where he also judged Israel and built an altar to the LORD.
When Samuel grew old, he appointed his sons to judge Israel.
His oldest son was Joel, and his second was Abijah. They served as judges in Beersheba.
His sons didn't follow his example. They went after dishonest gain, took bribes, and twisted justice.
All Israel's elders gathered and went to see Samuel at Ramah.
They told him, “You're old, and your sons don't follow your ways. Appoint a king to govern us, like all the other nations have.”
Samuel was upset when they asked for a king to govern them, so he prayed to the LORD.
The LORD told Samuel, “Listen to everything the people tell you. I'm the one they've rejected as their king. Their rejection is directed at me.
From the day I brought them out of Egypt until now, they've abandoned me and served other gods. Now they're treating you the same way.
So listen to them, but warn them plainly and tell them what the king who rules over them will do.”
Samuel passed on all the LORD's words to the people who'd asked him for a king.
He said, “Here's what the king who rules over you will do. He'll take your sons into his service, put them in his chariots and cavalry, and make some run ahead of his chariots.
He'll make some commanders over a thousand men and others over fifty. He'll make some plow his fields, harvest his crops, and make his weapons and chariot equipment.
He'll take your daughters to make perfume, cook, and bake for him.
He'll take the best of your fields, vineyards, and olive groves and give them to his servants.
He'll take a tenth of your grain and what your vineyards produce and give it to his officers and servants.
He'll take your male and female servants, your best young men, and your donkeys, and put them to work for him.
He'll take a tenth of your flocks, and you'll become his servants.
That day you'll cry out because of the king you chose for yourselves, and the LORD won't answer you.”
The people refused to listen to Samuel. They said, “No, we want a king over us.
Then we'll be like all the other nations. Our king will govern us, go out ahead of us, and fight our battles.”
Samuel heard everything the people said and repeated it to the LORD.
The LORD told him, “Listen to them and appoint a king for them.” Then Samuel told the people of Israel, “Everyone go back to your own town.”
There was a prominent man from Benjamin named Kish. He was the son of Abiel, son of Zeror, son of Becorath, son of Aphiah, a Benjaminite.
Kish had a son named Saul, an impressive young man. Nobody in Israel was more handsome than Saul, and he stood a head taller than everyone else.
One day Kish's donkeys went missing. He told Saul, “Take one of the servants with you and go look for the donkeys.”
They traveled through Ephraim's hill country and the land of Shalishah without finding them. They went through Shaalim and then through Benjamin's territory, but the donkeys were nowhere to be found.
When they reached the land of Zuph, Saul told his servant, “Let's go home before my father stops worrying about the donkeys and starts worrying about us.”
The servant said, “There's a man of God in this town. People respect him, and everything he says comes true. Let's go see him. Maybe he can tell us where to go.”
Saul asked, “If we go, what can we bring him? The bread in our bags is gone, and we haven't got a gift for the man of God. What do we have?”
The servant said, “I have a quarter shekel of silver. I'll give it to the man of God to show us where to go.”
In earlier days in Israel, when someone wanted to ask God for guidance, they'd say, “Let's go see the seer.” A prophet used to be called a seer.
Saul told his servant, “Good idea. Let's go.” So they headed to the town where the man of God was.
As they went uphill toward the town, they met some young women coming out to draw water and asked, “Is the seer here?”
They answered, “Yes, he's just ahead of you. Hurry. He came to town today because the people are offering a sacrifice at the high place.
When you get into town, you'll find him before he goes up to the high place to eat. The guests wait for him to bless the sacrifice before they eat. Go up now, and you'll find him.”
They went up to the town, and just as they entered, Samuel came out toward them on his way to the high place.
The day before Saul arrived, the LORD had told Samuel,
“Tomorrow about this time I'll send you a man from Benjamin. Anoint him as ruler over my people Israel. He'll rescue them from the Philistines. I've seen my people, and their cries have reached me.”
When Samuel saw Saul, the LORD said to him, “That's the man I told you about. He'll rule over my people.”
Saul approached Samuel at the gate and asked, “Can you tell me where the seer lives?”
Samuel said, “I'm the seer. Go ahead of me to the high place, because you'll eat with me today. In the morning I'll send you on your way and tell you everything that's on your mind.
Don't worry about the donkeys you lost three days ago. They've been found. And who is all Israel looking to? Isn't it you and your father's whole family?”
Saul answered, “I'm from Benjamin, the smallest tribe in Israel, and my family is the least important in Benjamin. Why are you talking to me like this?”
Samuel took Saul and his servant into the guest room and gave them the places of honor among about thirty guests.
Samuel told the cook, “Bring the serving I gave you and asked you to set aside.”

The cook brought out the thigh and what was on it and put it before Saul. Samuel said, “Here is the portion I had set aside. Eat it. It was kept for you for this occasion, when I invited these guests.” So Saul ate with Samuel that day.
After they came down from the high place into town, Samuel spoke with Saul on the roof.
They got up early. Around daybreak Samuel called to Saul on the roof, “Get up, and I'll send you on your way.” Saul got up, and the two went outside together.
As they reached the edge of town, Samuel told Saul to send the servant on ahead. After the servant went on, Samuel said, “Stay here a moment so I can tell you God's message.”
Samuel took a flask of oil, poured it on Saul's head, kissed him, and said, “The LORD has anointed you to rule over his inheritance.

When you leave me today, you'll meet two men near Rachel's tomb at Zelzah on Benjamin's border. They'll tell you the donkeys you went looking for have been found and that your father is now worried about you and asking what he should do about his son.

Then you'll go on to the oak of Tabor, where three men going up to worship God at Bethel will meet you. One will be carrying three young goats, another three loaves of bread, and another a container of wine.
They'll greet you and offer you two loaves. Take them.

After that you'll reach the hill of God, where the Philistines have a garrison. As you enter the town, you'll meet a group of prophets coming down from the high place. They'll be prophesying, with a lute, tambourine, pipe, and harp playing ahead of them.
The LORD's Spirit will come powerfully upon you. You'll prophesy with them and become a different man.
Once these signs happen, do what the situation calls for, because God is with you.
Go down to Gilgal ahead of me. I'll come down to offer burnt offerings and peace offerings. Wait seven days until I arrive and tell you what to do.”
As Saul turned to leave Samuel, God gave him a different heart. All those signs came true that day.
When Saul and his servant reached the hill, a group of prophets met him. God's Spirit came powerfully upon him, and he prophesied among them.
When everyone who'd known Saul saw him prophesying with the prophets, they asked each other, “What's happened to Kish's son? Is Saul one of the prophets too?”
A man from there asked, “And who's their father?” That's how the saying started: “Is Saul one of the prophets too?”
When Saul finished prophesying, he went to the high place.
Saul's uncle asked him and his servant, “Where did you go?” Saul answered, “To look for the donkeys. When we couldn't find them, we went to Samuel.”
His uncle said, “Please tell me what Samuel told you.”
Saul said, “He told us straight out that the donkeys had been found.” But he said nothing about what Samuel had told him about becoming king.
Samuel called the people together before the LORD at Mizpah.
He told Israel, “The LORD, the God of Israel, says, ‘I brought Israel up out of Egypt and rescued you from the Egyptians and every kingdom that oppressed you.’
But today you've rejected your God, the one who rescues you from all your troubles and disasters. You said, ‘No! Give us a king!’ Now present yourselves before the LORD by tribe and by clan.”
Samuel brought all Israel's tribes forward, and the tribe of Benjamin was chosen.
He brought Benjamin forward clan by clan, and the clan of Matri was chosen. Then Saul son of Kish was chosen, but when they went looking for him, they couldn't find him.
They asked the LORD again, “Has the man come here yet?” The LORD answered, “He's hiding among the baggage.”
They ran and brought him out. When he stood among the people, he was a head taller than everyone else.
Samuel asked, “Do you see the man the LORD has chosen? Nobody among the people is like him.” Everyone shouted, “Long live the king!”
Samuel explained the rules of the kingdom to the people, wrote them down in a book, and placed it before the LORD. Then he sent everyone home.
Saul went home to Gibeah too, and men whose hearts God had touched went with him.
Some troublemakers said, “How could this man save us?” They looked down on him and brought him no gift. Saul kept quiet.
Nahash the Ammonite went up and camped against Jabesh Gilead. The men of Jabesh told him, “Make a treaty with us, and we'll serve you.”
Nahash said, “I'll make a treaty on one condition. I'll gouge out your right eyes and bring disgrace on all Israel.”
The elders of Jabesh answered, “Give us seven days to send messengers throughout Israel. If nobody comes to rescue us, we'll come out to you.”
The messengers reached Saul's town of Gibeah and told the people what had happened. Everyone cried out and wept.
Saul was coming in from the fields behind his oxen. He asked, “What's wrong? Why is everyone crying?” They told him what the men of Jabesh had said.
When Saul heard it, God's Spirit came powerfully upon him, and he burned with anger.

He cut up a pair of oxen and sent the pieces throughout Israel with messengers. They announced, “This is what will happen to the oxen of anyone who refuses to follow Saul and Samuel.” The fear of the LORD fell on the people, and they came out together as one.
Saul counted them at Bezek. There were three hundred thousand men from Israel and thirty thousand from Judah.
They told the messengers, “Tell the people of Jabesh Gilead, ‘Tomorrow, by the time the sun is hot, you'll be rescued.’” When the messengers brought the news, the people of Jabesh were glad.
The people of Jabesh told Nahash, “Tomorrow we'll come out to you, and you can do whatever you think best with us.”

The next day Saul divided his men into three groups. They entered the camp during the morning watch and struck down the Ammonites until the heat of the day. The survivors scattered until no two were left together.
The people asked Samuel, “Who said Saul shouldn't rule over us? Bring those men here so we can put them to death.”
Saul said, “Nobody will be put to death today, because today the LORD has rescued Israel.”
Then Samuel told the people, “Come on, let's go to Gilgal and renew the kingdom there.”
Everyone went to Gilgal and made Saul king there before the LORD. They offered peace offerings to the LORD, and Saul and all the Israelites celebrated.
Samuel told all Israel, “I've listened to everything you asked of me and appointed a king over you.
Now your king leads you. I'm old and gray, and my sons are here among you. I've lived before you from my youth until today.

Here I am. Bring any charge against me before the LORD and his anointed king. Whose ox or donkey have I taken? Who have I cheated or oppressed? From whom have I taken a bribe to look the other way? I'll pay back anything I've taken.”
They answered, “You haven't cheated us, oppressed us, or taken anything from anybody.”
He said, “The LORD and his anointed one are witnesses today that you found nothing in my hands.” They answered, “He is our witness.”
Samuel said to the people, “The LORD appointed Moses and Aaron and brought your ancestors out of Egypt.
Stand here before the LORD while I remind you of all the righteous things he did for you and your ancestors.
After Jacob went down to Egypt, your ancestors cried out to the LORD. He sent Moses and Aaron, who brought them out of Egypt and settled them here.
But they forgot the LORD their God. So he sold them into the hands of Sisera, the commander of Hazor's army, the Philistines, and the king of Moab. All of them fought against your ancestors.
They cried out to the LORD, ‘We've sinned by abandoning the LORD and serving the Baals and the Ashtaroth. Rescue us from our enemies now, and we'll serve you.’
The LORD sent Jerubbaal, Bedan, Jephthah, and Samuel. He rescued you from enemies on every side, and you lived in safety.
But when you saw King Nahash of Ammon coming against you, you told me, ‘No, we want a king to rule over us,’ even though the LORD your God was already your king.
Now look at the king you chose and asked for. The LORD has set a king over you.
If you honor the LORD, serve him, listen to his voice, and obey his commands, then both you and the king who rules you will be following the LORD your God.
If you refuse to listen to the LORD and rebel against his commands, his hand will be against you, just as it was against your ancestors.
Now stand still and watch the great thing the LORD is about to do right in front of you.
Isn't it wheat harvest today? I'll call on the LORD to send thunder and rain, so you'll see for yourselves how wrong it was in his sight to ask for a king.”
Samuel called on the LORD, and the LORD sent thunder and rain that day. The people were in awe of the LORD and Samuel.
They told Samuel, “Pray to the LORD your God for us, your servants, so we don't die. We've added to all our sins by asking for a king.”
Samuel answered, “Don't be afraid. You really did all this wrong. Even so, keep following the LORD and serve him with your whole heart.
Don't turn aside to chase worthless things. They can't help you or save you, because they're empty.
For the honor of his great name, the LORD won't abandon his people. He was pleased to make you his own.
As for me, I'd be sinning against the LORD if I stopped praying for you. I'll keep teaching you the good and right way to live.
Honor the LORD and serve him faithfully with all your heart. Think about the great things he's done for you.
But if you keep doing evil, both you and your king will be swept away.”
Saul was thirty years old when he became king, and he ruled Israel for forty-two years.

Saul chose three thousand men from Israel. Two thousand stayed with him at Michmash and in the hills of Bethel, and a thousand stayed with Jonathan at Gibeah in Benjamin. Saul sent everyone else back to their tents.
Jonathan struck the Philistine garrison at Geba, and the Philistines heard about it. Saul had the trumpet blown throughout the land and said, “Let the Hebrews hear!”
All Israel heard that Saul had attacked the Philistine garrison and that the Philistines now hated Israel. The people rallied behind Saul at Gilgal.

The Philistines gathered to fight Israel with thirty thousand chariots, six thousand horsemen, and troops as numerous as grains of sand on the seashore. They went up and camped at Michmash, east of Beth Aven.
When the Israelites saw how much trouble they were in, they hid in caves, thickets, among rocks, in tombs, and in pits.
Some Hebrews crossed the Jordan into Gad and Gilead. Saul stayed at Gilgal, and the people still following him were trembling.
Saul waited seven days, the time Samuel had set. But Samuel didn't come to Gilgal, and the troops began scattering.
Saul said, “Bring me the burnt offering and the peace offerings.” Then he offered the burnt offering himself.
As soon as he finished offering it, Samuel arrived. Saul went out to greet him.
Samuel asked, “What have you done?” Saul answered, “I saw the men scattering. You hadn't come at the appointed time, and the Philistines had gathered at Michmash.
I thought, ‘The Philistines are about to come down against me at Gilgal, and I haven't asked for the LORD's favor.’ So I made myself go ahead and offer the burnt offering.”
Samuel told Saul, “You've acted foolishly. You didn't keep the command the LORD your God gave you. The LORD would have established your kingdom over Israel forever.
Now your kingdom won't last. The LORD has found a man after his own heart and appointed him ruler over his people, because you didn't keep what the LORD commanded you.”
Samuel left Gilgal and went to Gibeah in Benjamin. Saul counted the men still with him. There were about six hundred.
Saul, his son Jonathan, and the men with them stayed at Geba in Benjamin, while the Philistines camped at Michmash.
Raiding parties went out from the Philistine camp in three groups. One went toward Ophrah in the land of Shual.
Another headed toward Beth Horon, and the third went toward the border overlooking the Valley of Zeboim, out toward the wilderness.
There wasn't a blacksmith anywhere in Israel, because the Philistines wanted to keep the Hebrews from making swords or spears.
So the Israelites went down to the Philistines to have their plowshares, mattocks, axes, and sickles sharpened.
They charged one payim each to sharpen mattocks, plowshares, pitchforks, axes, and goads.
When the day of battle came, none of the men with Saul and Jonathan had a sword or spear. Saul and his son Jonathan were the only ones who had them.
The Philistine garrison went out to the pass at Michmash.
One day Jonathan son of Saul told his young armor-bearer, “Come with me to the Philistine outpost on the other side.” He didn't tell his father.
Saul was on the outskirts of Gibeah under the pomegranate tree at Migron. About six hundred men were with him.
Ahijah, who wore an ephod, was among them. He was the son of Ahitub, Ichabod's brother, son of Phinehas, son of Eli, the LORD's priest at Shiloh. The troops didn't know Jonathan had left.
There was a steep rock on either side of the pass Jonathan wanted to take to the Philistine outpost. One was called Bozez and the other Seneh.
One stood to the north facing Michmash, and the other stood to the south facing Geba.
Jonathan told his armor-bearer, “Come on. Let's cross to the outpost of these uncircumcised men. Maybe the LORD will act for us. Nothing keeps the LORD from saving by many or by few.”
His armor-bearer said, “Do whatever you have in mind. Go ahead. I'm with you all the way.”
Jonathan said, “We'll cross over and let those men see us.
If they tell us, ‘Wait there until we come to you,’ we'll stay where we are and won't go up.
If they say, ‘Come up to us,’ we'll go up, because the LORD has handed them over to us. That will be our sign.”
They showed themselves to the Philistine outpost. The Philistines said, “Look, the Hebrews are coming out of the holes where they've been hiding!”
The men at the outpost called to Jonathan and his armor-bearer, “Come up here and we'll show you something!” Jonathan told his armor-bearer, “Follow me up. The LORD has handed them over to Israel.”
Jonathan scrambled up on his hands and feet with his armor-bearer behind him. Men fell before Jonathan, and his armor-bearer followed, killing them.
In that first attack, Jonathan and his armor-bearer struck down about twenty men within roughly half a furrow's length in a field.
Panic spread through the camp, the field, the outpost, and the raiding parties. The earth shook, and everyone was terrified.
Saul's lookouts at Gibeah in Benjamin saw the Philistine army dissolve and scatter.
Saul told his men, “Count everyone and find out who's missing.” When they counted, Jonathan and his armor-bearer were gone.
Saul told Ahijah to bring God's ark, because the ark was with the Israelites at that time.
While Saul was speaking to the priest, the uproar in the Philistine camp grew louder. Saul told the priest, “Take your hand away!”
Saul and all his men rushed to the battle and found the Philistines in complete confusion, striking one another with their swords.
The Hebrews who had previously joined the Philistines in their camp switched sides and joined the Israelites with Saul and Jonathan.
When the Israelites who'd been hiding in Ephraim's hill country heard the Philistines were fleeing, they joined the pursuit too.
The LORD rescued Israel that day, and the fighting spread beyond Beth Aven.
The Israelites were in distress that day because Saul had put them under an oath: “Cursed is anyone who eats before evening, before I've taken revenge on my enemies.” So nobody tasted any food.
The whole army came into the woods, where there was honey on the ground.
They saw honey dripping, but no one tasted it because they were afraid of breaking the oath.
Jonathan hadn't heard his father's oath. He dipped the tip of his staff into the honeycomb and tasted the honey, and his eyes brightened.
One of the men told him, “Your father put everyone under a strict oath. He said, ‘Cursed is anyone who eats today.’” The men were exhausted.
Jonathan said, “My father has brought trouble on the land. Look how my eyes brightened after I tasted just a little honey.
How much better would it have been if everyone had eaten freely from what they took from their enemies today? We could have struck down many more Philistines.”
That day they struck down the Philistines from Michmash to Aijalon. The troops were worn out.
They rushed to the plunder, took sheep, cattle, and calves, and slaughtered them on the ground. Then they ate the meat with the blood still in it.
Someone told Saul, “The people are sinning against the LORD by eating meat with the blood.” Saul said, “You've broken faith. Roll a large stone over here now.”

He told his men to go through the crowd and say, “Bring your cattle and sheep here. Slaughter them here and eat, so you don't sin against the LORD by eating meat with the blood.” That night everyone brought their cattle and slaughtered them there.
Saul built an altar to the LORD. It was the first altar he'd built for him.
Saul said, “Let's pursue the Philistines by night and plunder them until dawn. Leave none of them alive.” The men answered, “Do whatever seems right to you.” The priest said, “Let's ask God first.”
Saul asked God, “Should I go after the Philistines? Will you hand them over to Israel?” But God didn't answer him that day.
Saul said, “Come here, all you leaders. Let's find out who's responsible for today's sin.
As surely as the LORD who rescues Israel lives, even if my own son Jonathan is guilty, he will die.” Nobody answered him.
Saul told all Israel, “Stand over on one side. My son Jonathan and I will stand on the other.” The people said, “Do what seems right to you.”
Saul prayed to the LORD, the God of Israel, “Show us who is in the right.” Saul and Jonathan were selected, and the people were cleared.
Saul said, “Cast lots between me and my son Jonathan.” Jonathan was selected.
Saul told Jonathan, “Tell me what you did.” Jonathan answered, “I tasted a little honey from the end of my staff. And now I have to die.”
Saul said, “May God deal with me severely if you don't die, Jonathan.”

The people told Saul, “Should Jonathan die after bringing Israel this great victory? Never! As surely as the LORD lives, not one hair of his head will fall to the ground. He worked with God today.” So the people rescued Jonathan, and he didn't die.
Saul stopped pursuing the Philistines, and they went back to their own land.
After taking the throne of Israel, Saul fought enemies on every side: Moab, Ammon, Edom, the kings of Zobah, and the Philistines. Wherever he turned, he defeated them.
He fought bravely and struck down the Amalekites, rescuing Israel from those who had been plundering them.
Saul's sons were Jonathan, Ishvi, and Malchishua. His older daughter was Merab, and his younger daughter was Michal.
Saul's wife was Ahinoam daughter of Ahimaaz. Abner son of Ner, Saul's uncle, commanded his army.
Kish was Saul's father, and Ner, Abner's father, was the son of Abiel.
The fighting against the Philistines was fierce throughout Saul's life. Whenever he saw a strong or brave man, he recruited him into his service.
Samuel told Saul, “The LORD sent me to anoint you as king over his people Israel. Now listen to what the LORD says.
The LORD of Armies says, ‘I remember what Amalek did to Israel, how they came against them on the road out of Egypt.
Go and strike Amalek. Destroy everything they have and spare no one, whether man or woman, infant or nursing baby, cattle or sheep, camel or donkey.’”
Saul called the people together and counted them at Telaim. There were two hundred thousand foot soldiers and ten thousand men from Judah.
Saul went to the city of Amalek and set an ambush in the valley.
He told the Kenites, “Get away from the Amalekites, or you could be destroyed along with them. You showed kindness to all Israel when they came out of Egypt.” So they left.
Saul struck down the Amalekites from Havilah as far as Shur, east of Egypt.
He took King Agag of Amalek alive and put all the people to the sword.
Saul and his troops spared Agag and the best sheep, cattle, fat calves, and lambs. They kept everything they thought was good and destroyed only what they considered worthless.
Then the LORD's word came to Samuel.
“I regret making Saul king. He's turned away from following me and hasn't done what I commanded.” Samuel was angry and cried out to the LORD all night.
Early the next morning Samuel went to meet Saul. Someone told him, “Saul went to Carmel and set up a monument to himself. Then he moved on down to Gilgal.”
When Samuel reached him, Saul said, “May the LORD bless you! I've done what the LORD commanded.”
Samuel asked, “Then why do I hear sheep bleating and cattle lowing?”
Saul answered, “The troops brought them from the Amalekites. They saved the best sheep and cattle to sacrifice to the LORD your God. We destroyed the rest.”
Samuel said, “Stop. Let me tell you what the LORD said to me last night.” Saul said, “Go ahead.”
Samuel said, “You used to think little of yourself, yet you became the head of Israel's tribes. The LORD anointed you king over Israel.
The LORD sent you on a mission and told you to fight the Amalekites for their sins and destroy them completely.
Why didn't you listen to the LORD? Why did you seize the plunder and do what was evil in his sight?”
Saul told Samuel, “I did listen to the LORD. I went where he sent me, brought back Agag king of Amalek, and destroyed the Amalekites.
The troops took sheep and cattle from the plunder, the best of what had been set apart, to sacrifice to the LORD your God at Gilgal.”
Samuel said, “Does the LORD delight in burnt offerings and sacrifices as much as he delights in obedience? Obedience is better than sacrifice, and listening is better than the fat of rams.
Rebellion is like witchcraft, and stubbornness is like worshiping idols and household gods. Because you rejected the LORD's word, he has rejected you as king.”
Saul said, “I've sinned. I broke the LORD's command and ignored your words because I was afraid of the people and listened to them.
Please forgive my sin and come back with me so I can worship the LORD.”
Samuel answered, “I won't go back with you. You rejected the LORD's word, and the LORD has rejected you as king over Israel.”
As Samuel turned to leave, Saul grabbed the edge of his robe, and it tore.
Samuel told him, “Today the LORD has torn the kingdom of Israel away from you and given it to someone close to you who is better than you.
The Strength of Israel doesn't lie or change his mind. He isn't human, so he doesn't change his mind as people do.”
Saul said, “I've sinned. Please still honor me before my people's elders and before Israel. Come back with me so I can worship the LORD your God.”
Samuel returned with Saul, and Saul worshiped the LORD.
Then Samuel said, “Bring me Agag, the king of the Amalekites.” Agag came to him cheerfully and said, “Surely the bitterness of death has passed.”
Samuel said, “Your sword has left women childless. Now your mother will be childless too.” Then Samuel executed Agag before the LORD at Gilgal.
Samuel went back to Ramah, and Saul went home to Gibeah of Saul.
Samuel never went to see Saul again before his death, but he mourned for him. The LORD regretted making Saul king over Israel.

The LORD told Samuel, “How long will you grieve for Saul? I've rejected him as king over Israel. Fill your horn with oil and go. I'm sending you to Jesse of Bethlehem, because I've chosen one of his sons to be my king.”
Samuel asked, “How can I go? If Saul hears about it, he'll kill me.” The LORD said, “Take a young cow with you and say, ‘I've come to sacrifice to the LORD.’
Invite Jesse to the sacrifice. I'll show you what to do. Anoint the one I point out to you.”
Samuel did what the LORD said and went to Bethlehem. The town elders came out trembling to meet him and asked, “Have you come in peace?”
He said, “Yes, I've come in peace to sacrifice to the LORD. Set yourselves apart and come with me to the sacrifice.” He set Jesse and his sons apart and invited them to come.
When they arrived and Samuel saw Eliab, he thought, “Surely this is the one the LORD has chosen to anoint.”
But the LORD told Samuel, “Don't judge by his looks or how tall he is. I've rejected him. I see differently from people. People look at what's on the outside, but the LORD looks at the heart.”
Jesse called Abinadab forward and had him pass in front of Samuel. Samuel said, “The LORD hasn't chosen this one either.”
Then Jesse brought Shammah forward. Samuel said, “The LORD hasn't chosen him either.”
Jesse brought seven of his sons before Samuel, but Samuel said, “The LORD hasn't chosen any of these.”
Samuel asked, “Are these all your sons?” Jesse said, “There's still the youngest, but he's out looking after the sheep.” Samuel said, “Send for him. We won't sit down until he gets here.”
Jesse sent for him. The boy had a ruddy complexion, a handsome face, and a striking appearance. The LORD said, “Get up and anoint him. He's the one.”
Samuel took the horn of oil and anointed David in front of his brothers. From that day on, the LORD's Spirit came powerfully upon David. Then Samuel left for Ramah.
The LORD's Spirit left Saul, and an evil spirit from the LORD tormented him.
Saul's servants told him, “An evil spirit from God is tormenting you.
Give your servants the order to look for someone who plays the harp well. When the evil spirit from God comes over you, he can play and you'll feel better.”
Saul told them, “Find someone who plays well and bring him to me.”
One of the young men answered, “I've seen a son of Jesse from Bethlehem who plays well. He's brave, he knows how to fight, he speaks wisely, and he's handsome. The LORD is with him.”
Saul sent messengers to Jesse. “Send me your son David, the one who looks after the sheep.”
Jesse loaded a donkey with bread, a container of wine, and a young goat and sent his son David to Saul with them.
David came and entered Saul's service. Saul grew very fond of him, and David became his armor-bearer.
Saul sent word to Jesse, “Please let David stay in my service. He's found favor with me.”
Whenever the spirit from God came over Saul, David took his harp and played. Saul felt better and found relief, and the evil spirit left him.
The Philistines gathered their armies for battle at Socoh in Judah and camped between Socoh and Azekah at Ephesdammim.
Saul and the Israelites gathered in the Valley of Elah and lined up for battle against the Philistines.
The Philistines stood on one hill, Israel stood on the other, and the valley lay between them.
A champion named Goliath, from Gath, stepped out of the Philistine camp. He was six cubits and a span tall.
He wore a bronze helmet and a coat of armor that weighed five thousand shekels of bronze.
He wore bronze guards on his shins and carried a bronze javelin across his shoulders.
His spear shaft was like a weaver's beam, and its iron point weighed six hundred shekels. His shield-bearer walked ahead of him.
He stood and shouted to Israel's army, “Why have you lined up for battle? I'm a Philistine, and you serve Saul. Choose one man to come down and face me.
If he fights me and kills me, we'll serve you. But if I beat him and kill him, you'll serve us.”
The Philistine said, “Today I defy Israel's army! Send me a man, and let us fight!”
When Saul and all Israel heard him, they lost heart and were terrified.
David was the son of Jesse, an Ephrathite from Bethlehem in Judah. Jesse had eight sons and was already an old man in Saul's time.
Jesse's three oldest sons had gone to battle with Saul: Eliab the firstborn, Abinadab the second, and Shammah the third.
David was the youngest. The three oldest followed Saul.
David went back and forth from Saul to Bethlehem to look after his father's sheep.
For forty days, morning and evening, the Philistine came forward to issue his challenge.
Jesse told his son David, “Take an ephah of this roasted grain and these ten loaves and hurry to the camp with them for your brothers.
Take these ten cheeses to their commander. See how your brothers are doing and bring me word.”
Saul, David's brothers, and the Israelites were in the Valley of Elah fighting the Philistines.
David got up early, left the sheep with a keeper, and took the supplies as Jesse had told him. He reached the wagons as the army was marching out and shouting its battle cry.
Israel and the Philistines lined up across from each other.
David left his things with the man in charge of the supplies, ran to the battle line, and greeted his brothers.
As he spoke with them, Goliath of Gath, the Philistine champion, came forward and repeated his challenge. David heard him.
When the Israelites saw Goliath, they were terrified and ran from him.
They said, “Do you see that man? He's come out to defy Israel. The king will make whoever kills him rich, give him his daughter in marriage, and exempt his father's household from taxes in Israel.”
David asked the men nearby, “What will be done for the man who kills this Philistine and takes away Israel's disgrace? Who is this uncircumcised Philistine to defy the armies of the living God?”
They repeated what would be done for whoever killed him.

David's oldest brother Eliab heard him speaking and was furious. “Why did you come down here? Who's looking after those few sheep in the wilderness? I know how proud you are and what you're really after. You came to watch the battle.”
David said, “What did I do now? Isn't there a reason to ask?”
He turned to someone else and asked the same question, and the people gave him the same answer.
When word of what David had said reached Saul, Saul sent for him.
David told Saul, “Nobody should lose heart because of this man. I'll go fight this Philistine.”
Saul answered, “You can't go out against him. You're only a boy, and he's been a warrior since he was young.”
David said, “I look after my father's sheep. When a lion or a bear carried off a lamb,
I went after it, struck it, and rescued the lamb from its mouth. When the animal turned on me, I grabbed it by the beard, struck it, and killed it.
I've killed both lions and bears. This uncircumcised Philistine will end up like one of them because he's defied the armies of the living God.
The LORD rescued me from the lion and the bear. He'll rescue me from this Philistine too.” Saul said, “Go, and the LORD be with you.”
Saul dressed David in his own gear. He put a bronze helmet on David's head and a coat of armor on his body.
David strapped the sword on and tried to walk, but he wasn't used to the gear. He told Saul, “I can't go in this. I've never used it.” So he took it off.
David took his staff, picked five smooth stones from the stream, and put them in his shepherd's bag. With his sling in hand, he went toward the Philistine.
The Philistine came closer to David, with his shield-bearer walking ahead.
When Goliath looked at David, he looked down on him because he was young, ruddy, and handsome.
He said, “Am I a dog, that you come at me with sticks?” Then he cursed David by his gods.
The Philistine said, “Come here, and I'll feed your flesh to the birds and wild animals.”
David answered, “You come at me with a sword, spear, and javelin. I come at you in the name of the LORD of Armies, the God of Israel's armies, whom you've defied.

Today the LORD will hand you over to me. I'll strike you down and cut off your head. I'll give the bodies of the Philistine army to the birds and wild animals today, so everyone on earth will know there is a God in Israel.
Everyone gathered here will know that the LORD saves without sword or spear. The battle belongs to the LORD, and he'll hand you over to us.”
As the Philistine came forward to face him, David ran out to meet him.
David took a stone from his bag and slung it at the Philistine. The stone struck him in the forehead, and he fell facedown to the ground.
David defeated and killed the Philistine with a sling and a stone. He didn't have a sword in his hand.
David ran up, stood over the Philistine, and drew the man's own sword. He killed him and cut off his head. When the Philistines saw that their champion was dead, they ran.
The men of Israel and Judah rose with a shout and chased the Philistines to Gai and the gates of Ekron. The wounded fell along the road to Shaaraim, as far as Gath and Ekron.
When the Israelites came back from chasing the Philistines, they plundered their camp.
David took the Philistine's head to Jerusalem, but put the man's armor in his own tent.
When Saul saw David go out against the Philistine, he asked Abner, his army commander, “Abner, whose son is that boy?” Abner answered, “As surely as you live, my king, I don't know.”
The king told him, “Find out whose son he is.”
When David returned from killing the Philistine, Abner brought him before Saul, still carrying the Philistine's head.
Saul asked him, “Whose son are you, young man?” David replied, “I'm the son of your servant Jesse of Bethlehem.”
When David finished speaking with Saul, Jonathan felt deeply bound to David and loved him as he loved himself.
From that day Saul kept David with him and no longer let him go back to his father's house.
Jonathan made a covenant with David because he loved him as he loved himself.
Jonathan took off his robe and gave it to David, along with his clothes, sword, bow, and belt.
David went wherever Saul sent him and acted wisely. Saul put him in charge of fighting men, and this pleased both the people and Saul's servants.
When David came back from killing the Philistine, women from all over Israel came out to greet King Saul. They sang and danced with tambourines and other instruments, celebrating.
As they played, the women sang to one another, “Saul has killed his thousands, and David his tens of thousands.”
Saul was furious. He said, “They've given David credit for tens of thousands and me for just thousands. What more can he get except the kingdom?”
From then on Saul kept a suspicious eye on David.
The next day an evil spirit from God came powerfully over Saul, and he prophesied inside the house. David played as he did every day, and Saul held a spear.
Saul hurled the spear, thinking, “I'll pin David to the wall.” David escaped him twice.
Saul was afraid of David because the LORD was with David and had left Saul.
So Saul sent David away from his presence and put him in command of a thousand men. David led the troops out and brought them back.
David acted wisely in everything he did, and the LORD was with him.
When Saul saw how wisely David acted, he became even more afraid of him.
All Israel and Judah loved David because he led them out and brought them back.

Saul told David, “Here's my older daughter Merab. I'll give her to you as your wife. Just be brave in my service and fight the LORD's battles.” Saul was thinking, “I'll let the Philistines kill him so I don't have to.”
David asked, “Who am I, and what standing do I or my father's family have in Israel, that I should become the king's son-in-law?”
When the time came for Saul's daughter Merab to marry David, she was given to Adriel the Meholathite instead.
Saul's daughter Michal loved David. When Saul heard, the news pleased him.
He thought, “I'll give her to David, and she'll become a trap for him. Then the Philistines can get him.” So Saul told David a second time, “Today you'll become my son-in-law.”
Saul told his servants to speak privately to David and say, “The king likes you, and all his servants love you. Now go ahead and become his son-in-law.”
When the servants told David, he replied, “Do you think becoming the king's son-in-law is a small thing? I'm poor and hardly anyone knows me.”
Saul's servants reported what David had said.
Saul said, “Tell David the king asks for no bride price except a hundred Philistine foreskins as revenge on his enemies.” Saul hoped the Philistines would kill David.
When the servants told David, he was pleased at the chance to become the king's son-in-law. Before the deadline,

David and his men went out and killed two hundred Philistines. David brought back their foreskins and gave the full number to the king to become his son-in-law. Then Saul gave him his daughter Michal in marriage.
Saul saw that the LORD was with David and knew that his daughter Michal loved him.
Saul became even more afraid of David, and from then on he was always David's enemy.
Whenever the Philistine commanders came out to fight, David acted more wisely than all Saul's other officers. His name became widely respected.
Saul told his son Jonathan and all his servants to kill David. But Jonathan cared deeply about David.
He warned him, “My father Saul is trying to kill you. Be careful in the morning, and stay hidden somewhere safe.
I'll go out and stand beside my father in the field where you're hiding. I'll talk to him about you and tell you what I find out.”
Jonathan spoke well of David to his father. He said, “The king shouldn't wrong his servant David. David hasn't wronged you, and what he's done has been very good for you.
He risked his life and struck down the Philistine, and the LORD won a great victory for all Israel. You saw it and celebrated. Why would you shed innocent blood and kill David for no reason?”
Saul listened to Jonathan and swore, “As surely as the LORD lives, David won't be put to death.”
Jonathan called David and told him everything. Then he brought David back to Saul, and David served in his presence as before.
War broke out again. David went out and fought the Philistines, striking them down in great numbers. They fled from him.
An evil spirit from the LORD came upon Saul as he sat in his house with his spear in his hand. David was playing music.
Saul tried to pin David to the wall with the spear. David slipped away, and the spear stuck in the wall. David ran and escaped that night.
Saul sent men to watch David's house and kill him in the morning. David's wife Michal warned him, “If you don't get away tonight, you'll be killed tomorrow.”
Michal lowered David through the window. He ran away and escaped.
Michal put a household idol in the bed, placed a goats' hair pillow at its head, and covered it with clothes.
When Saul sent men to take David, Michal told them, “He's sick.”
Saul sent the men back to see David. “Bring him to me in his bed so I can kill him.”
When they went in, they found the household idol in the bed with the goats' hair pillow at its head.
Saul asked Michal, “Why did you trick me like this and let my enemy get away?” Michal answered, “He told me, ‘Let me go! Why should I kill you?’”
David escaped to Samuel at Ramah and told him everything Saul had done to him. David and Samuel went and stayed at Naioth.
Someone told Saul, “David is at Naioth in Ramah.”
Saul sent men to seize David. When they saw the group of prophets prophesying with Samuel leading them, God's Spirit came upon Saul's men, and they prophesied too.
When Saul heard, he sent other men, and they prophesied too. Saul sent a third group, and they also prophesied.
Then Saul went to Ramah himself. At the large well in Secu he asked, “Where are Samuel and David?” Someone answered, “At Naioth in Ramah.”
Saul headed there, and God's Spirit came upon him too. He kept prophesying as he went until he reached Naioth in Ramah.
He took off his clothes and prophesied before Samuel. He lay naked all that day and night. That's why people say, “Is Saul one of the prophets too?”
David fled from Naioth in Ramah and went to Jonathan. “What have I done? What's my crime? How have I wronged your father that he wants to kill me?”
Jonathan answered, “No, you won't die. My father doesn't do anything, big or small, without telling me. Why would he hide this from me? It can't be true.”

David swore, “Your father knows you care about me. He's thinking, ‘Don't tell Jonathan, or he'll be upset.’ But as surely as the LORD lives and as surely as you live, I'm only one step away from death.”
Jonathan told David, “Whatever you need, I'll do it for you.”
David said, “Tomorrow is the new moon, and I'm supposed to eat with the king. Let me hide in the field until the evening of the third day.
If your father notices I'm missing, say, ‘David asked me urgently for permission to go to Bethlehem, his hometown, because his whole family is holding its annual sacrifice there.’
If he says that's fine, I'll be safe. If he gets angry, you'll know he's determined to hurt me.
Show me kindness, because you brought me into a covenant with you before the LORD. If I've done wrong, kill me yourself. Why hand me over to your father?”
Jonathan said, “I'd never do that to you. If I find out my father has decided to hurt you, of course I'll tell you.”
David asked, “Who will tell me if your father answers you harshly?”
Jonathan said, “Come on, let's go out to the field.” So they went out together.
Jonathan told David, “By the LORD, the God of Israel, I'll find out what my father thinks by this time tomorrow or the third day. If he's well disposed toward you, I'll send word and tell you.
If my father intends to hurt you, may the LORD deal severely with me if I don't warn you and send you away safely. May the LORD be with you as he was with my father.
While I'm still alive, show me the LORD's faithful love so I don't die.
Keep showing kindness to my family forever, even after the LORD has removed every one of your enemies from the face of the earth.”
Jonathan made a covenant with David's family and said, “May the LORD hold David's enemies to account.”
Jonathan had David swear again because he loved him as much as he loved himself.
Then Jonathan said, “Tomorrow is the new moon. They'll notice you're missing when your seat is empty.
On the third day, go quickly to the place where you hid when this first happened and stay by the stone called Ezel.
I'll shoot three arrows beside it as if I were aiming at a target.
I'll send the boy to find the arrows. If I tell him, ‘The arrows are on this side of you. Pick them up,’ you can come out. As surely as the LORD lives, you're safe and there's no danger.
But if I tell him, ‘The arrows are beyond you,’ go on your way, because the LORD has sent you away.
As for what you and I have promised, the LORD stands between us forever.”
David hid in the field. When the new moon came, the king sat down for the meal.
Saul sat in his usual place by the wall. Jonathan stood up, and Abner sat beside Saul. David's seat was empty.
Saul said nothing that day. He thought, “Something must have happened to make him unclean. That has to be it.”
On the second day of the new moon, David's seat was still empty. Saul asked Jonathan, “Why hasn't Jesse's son come to eat, either yesterday or today?”
Jonathan answered, “David asked me urgently for permission to go to Bethlehem.

He said, ‘Please let me go. Our family is offering a sacrifice in town, and my brother told me to be there. If I've found favor with you, please let me go see my brothers.’ That's why he hasn't come to your table.”
Saul flew into a rage at Jonathan. “You son of a rebellious, twisted woman! I know you've chosen Jesse's son, bringing shame on yourself and on the mother who bore you.
As long as Jesse's son is alive, neither you nor your kingdom will stand. Send for him and bring him to me. He has to die!”
Jonathan asked his father, “Why should he be put to death? What has he done?”
Saul hurled his spear at Jonathan to strike him. Then Jonathan knew his father was determined to kill David.
Jonathan got up from the table furious and ate nothing that second day of the month. He grieved for David because his father had treated him so shamefully.
The next morning Jonathan went to the field at the time he'd agreed on with David. A young boy went with him.
He told the boy, “Run and find the arrows I shoot.” As the boy ran, Jonathan shot an arrow beyond him.
When the boy reached the place where the arrow had landed, Jonathan called, “Isn't the arrow farther ahead?”
Jonathan shouted, “Hurry! Keep going!” The boy gathered the arrows and brought them back.
The boy knew nothing about what was going on. Only Jonathan and David knew.
Jonathan handed his weapons to the boy and told him to take them back to town.
As soon as the boy left, David came out from the south and bowed facedown to the ground three times. They kissed each other and wept together, with David weeping the most.

Jonathan told David, “Go in peace. We've both sworn in the LORD's name: ‘The LORD is between you and me and between your children and mine forever.’” David got up and left, and Jonathan went back into town.
David went to Nob to see Ahimelech the priest. Ahimelech came out trembling to meet him and asked, “Why are you alone? Why isn't anyone with you?”
David said, “The king sent me on a mission and told me to tell nobody what he sent me to do. I've arranged for my men to meet me at a certain place.
What do you have on hand? Please give me five loaves of bread, or whatever you have.”
The priest said, “I don't have any ordinary bread. I have holy bread, if the young men have kept away from women.”
David answered, “We've stayed away from women for these three days, as we usually do. My men's bodies were holy when we set out, even on an ordinary journey. How much more so today?”
So the priest gave him the holy bread. There was no other bread there except the bread that had been set before the LORD and removed that day to make room for fresh, hot bread.
One of Saul's servants was there that day, detained before the LORD. His name was Doeg the Edomite, and he was Saul's chief herdsman.
David asked Ahimelech, “Do you have a spear or sword here? I didn't bring my sword or any of my weapons, because the king's business was urgent.”

The priest said, “Goliath the Philistine's sword, the one you took when you killed him in the Valley of Elah, is wrapped in a cloth behind the ephod. Take it if you want it. It's the only one here.” David said, “There's no sword like it. Give it to me.”
That day David fled from Saul and went to King Achish of Gath.
Achish's servants said, “Isn't this David, the king of the land? Didn't the people dance and sing, ‘Saul has killed his thousands, and David his tens of thousands’?”
David took their words to heart and became very afraid of King Achish of Gath.
So he changed his behavior in front of them and pretended to have lost his mind while he was in their hands. He scratched on the gate doors and let saliva run down his beard.
Achish told his servants, “Look at him. You can see he's lost his mind. Why did you bring him here?
Don't I have enough people acting like this already? Did you have to bring this fellow to act like that in front of me? Should I let him into my house?”
David left Gath and escaped to the cave of Adullam. When his brothers and his father's whole family heard, they went down to join him.
Everyone in trouble, in debt, or bitter about their situation gathered around him. He became their leader, with about four hundred men under him.
From there David went to Mizpeh in Moab. He asked the king of Moab, “Please let my father and mother stay with you until I know what God will do for me.”
He brought them before the king of Moab, and they stayed with him the whole time David was in the stronghold.
The prophet Gad told David, “Don't stay in the stronghold. Go into the land of Judah.” So David left and went into the forest of Hereth.
Saul heard that David and his men had been found. Saul was sitting in Gibeah under the tamarisk tree at Ramah, spear in hand, with all his servants standing around him.
Saul said, “Listen, you men of Benjamin! Will Jesse's son give each of you fields and vineyards? Will he make you commanders over thousands or hundreds?

Is that why you've all conspired against me? Nobody told me when my son made a covenant with Jesse's son. Nobody feels sorry for me or tells me that my son has stirred up my servant to lie in wait against me, as he's doing today.”
Doeg the Edomite was standing with Saul's servants. He said, “I saw Jesse's son go to Nob to see Ahimelech son of Ahitub.
Ahimelech asked the LORD for guidance for him, gave him food, and gave him the sword of Goliath the Philistine.”
The king sent for Ahimelech the priest, son of Ahitub, and his father's whole household, the priests at Nob. They all came before the king.
Saul said, “Listen, son of Ahitub.” He answered, “Here I am, my lord.”
Saul asked, “Why have you and Jesse's son plotted against me? You gave him bread and a sword and asked God for guidance for him, so he could rise up and lie in wait against me, as he's doing today.”
Ahimelech answered, “Which of all your servants is as faithful as David? He's the king's son-in-law, captain of your guard, and honored in your household.
Was that the first time I asked God for him? Of course not. Please don't blame me or anyone in my father's family. I didn't know a thing about any of this.”
The king said, “You will die, Ahimelech, you and your father's whole household.”
The king told his guards, “Turn and kill the LORD's priests. They're on David's side. They knew he'd fled and didn't tell me.” But the king's servants refused to attack the LORD's priests.
Then the king ordered Doeg to attack the priests. Doeg the Edomite killed eighty-five men who wore the linen ephod that day.
He put Nob, the city of the priests, to the sword, killing men and women, children and nursing babies, and cattle, donkeys, and sheep.
Abiathar, one of the sons of Ahimelech son of Ahitub, escaped and fled to David.
He told David that Saul had killed the LORD's priests.
David told Abiathar, “When I saw Doeg the Edomite there that day, I knew he'd tell Saul. I'm responsible for the deaths of everyone in your father's household.
Stay with me. Don't be afraid. The man who wants to kill me wants to kill you too. You'll be safe with me.”
Word reached David that the Philistines were attacking Keilah and stealing grain from the threshing floors.
David asked the LORD, “Should I go and attack these Philistines?” The LORD answered, “Go, strike them down, and rescue Keilah.”
David's men told him, “We're afraid even here in Judah. How much worse will it be if we go to Keilah to face the Philistine army?”
David asked the LORD again. The LORD answered, “Get up and go down to Keilah. I'll hand the Philistines over to you.”
David and his men went to Keilah, fought the Philistines, and took their livestock. They struck them down in great numbers and rescued the people of Keilah.
When Abiathar son of Ahimelech fled to David at Keilah, he brought an ephod with him.
When Saul heard David had gone to Keilah, he said, “God has handed him over to me. He's trapped himself by going into a town with gates and bars.”
Saul called up all the troops to go down to Keilah and besiege David and his men.
David knew Saul was plotting against him. He told Abiathar the priest, “Bring the ephod here.”
Then David prayed, “LORD, God of Israel, I've heard that Saul intends to come to Keilah and destroy the town because of me.
Will the people of Keilah hand me over? Will Saul come down, as I've heard? LORD, God of Israel, please tell me.” The LORD answered, “He'll come down.”
David asked, “Will the people of Keilah hand me and my men over to Saul?” The LORD answered, “They'll hand you over.”
David and his men, about six hundred in all, left Keilah and went wherever they could. When Saul heard David had escaped, he called off the trip.
David stayed in wilderness strongholds and in the hills of the wilderness of Ziph. Saul looked for him every day, but God didn't hand David over to him.
David knew Saul had come out to kill him. At the time, David was in the woods in the wilderness of Ziph.
Jonathan son of Saul went to see David in the woods and helped him find strength in God.
He told him, “Don't be afraid. My father Saul won't get his hands on you. You'll be king over Israel, and I'll be at your side. Even my father knows that.”
The two made a covenant before the LORD. David stayed in the woods, and Jonathan went home.
Some people from Ziph went to Saul at Gibeah and told him, “David is hiding in our territory, in the strongholds in the woods on the hill of Hachilah, south of the desert.
Come down whenever you're ready, King, and we'll hand him over to you.”
Saul said, “May the LORD bless you for having compassion on me.
Go and make certain where he's staying and who has seen him there. I've been told he's very clever.
Find out all the places he hides, then come back when you're sure. I'll go with you. If he's in the land, I'll search him out among all the clans of Judah.”
They set out for Ziph ahead of Saul. David and his men were in the wilderness of Maon, in the Arabah south of the desert.
Saul and his men went looking for David. When David heard, he went down to the rock in the wilderness of Maon and stayed there. Saul heard about it and went after him.
Saul went along one side of the mountain while David and his men went along the other. David hurried to get away as Saul and his men closed in to capture them.
Then a messenger came to Saul. “Come quickly! The Philistines have raided the land!”
Saul broke off his pursuit of David and went to fight the Philistines. That's why the place was called Sela Hammahlekoth.
David left that place and stayed in the strongholds of En Gedi.
After Saul returned from chasing the Philistines, he heard that David was in the wilderness of En Gedi.
Saul took three thousand chosen men from all Israel and went looking for David and his men near the Rocks of the Wild Goats.
