He came to some sheep pens along the road and went into a cave to relieve himself. David and his men were deep inside the same cave.

David's men said, “This is the day the LORD told you about when he said, ‘I'll hand your enemy over to you, and you can do whatever seems right to you.’” David got up quietly and cut off the edge of Saul's robe.
Afterward David felt guilty for cutting the edge of Saul's robe.
He told his men, “May the LORD keep me from doing such a thing to my lord. I won't raise my hand against him, because he's the LORD's anointed.”
David held his men back with those words and wouldn't let them attack Saul. Saul got up, left the cave, and went on his way.
Then David came out of the cave and called after Saul, “My lord the king!” When Saul looked back, David bowed low with his face to the ground.
David asked, “Why do you listen to people who tell you I'm trying to hurt you?

Today you can see for yourself that the LORD handed you over to me in that cave. Some urged me to kill you, but I spared you. I said I wouldn't raise my hand against my lord because he's the LORD's anointed.

Look, my father. Here's the edge of your robe in my hand. I cut it off without killing you. This shows I'm doing you no wrong and haven't rebelled against you. I haven't sinned against you, even though you're hunting me down to kill me.
May the LORD judge between us and take vengeance for me, but I won't lay a hand on you.
As the old saying goes, ‘Wicked deeds come from wicked people.’ My hand will never be raised against you.
Who has the king of Israel come out to chase? Who are you after? A dead dog? A flea?
May the LORD judge between us, see what's happening, plead my case, and rescue me from you.”
When David finished speaking, Saul said, “Is that your voice, my son David?” Then Saul broke down and wept.
He said, “You're more righteous than I am. You've done good to me, while I've done you harm.
Today you've shown me how well you've treated me. The LORD handed me over to you, and you didn't kill me.
When someone finds his enemy, does he let him go unharmed? May the LORD reward you for what you've done for me today.
I know now that you'll become king and that the kingdom of Israel will be established in your hands.
Swear to me by the LORD that you won't cut off my descendants after me or erase my name from my father's family.”
David swore to Saul. Saul went home, and David and his men went up to the stronghold.
Samuel died, and all Israel gathered to mourn him. They buried him at his home in Ramah. Then David went down to the wilderness of Paran.
There was a wealthy man from Maon who owned property in Carmel. He had three thousand sheep and a thousand goats, and he was shearing his sheep in Carmel.
His name was Nabal, and his wife's name was Abigail. She was intelligent and beautiful, but he was harsh and acted badly. He belonged to Caleb's family.
While David was in the wilderness, he heard that Nabal was shearing his sheep.
David sent ten young men. He told them, “Go up to Carmel, find Nabal, and greet him for me.
Tell him, ‘Long life to you! May you, your family, and all that you have enjoy peace.
I hear it's shearing time. Your shepherds were with us, and we never harmed them. Nothing of theirs went missing the whole time they were at Carmel.
Ask your young men, and they'll tell you. Please welcome my men, because we've come on a day of celebration. Give whatever you can spare to your servants and to your son David.’”
David's men arrived, delivered his whole message to Nabal, and waited.
Nabal answered, “Who's David? Who's this son of Jesse? There are plenty of servants running away from their masters these days.
Why should I take my bread, my water, and the meat I prepared for my shearers and give it to strangers from who knows where?”
David's men turned around and went back to tell him everything Nabal had said.
David ordered his men to put on their swords. They did, and David put on his own sword. About four hundred followed David, while two hundred stayed with the supplies.
Meanwhile, one of Nabal's young servants told Abigail, “David sent messengers out of the wilderness to greet our master, and he insulted them.
Those men treated us well. They never harmed us, and nothing went missing the whole time we were with them in the fields.
They were like a wall around us day and night while we looked after the sheep near them.
Think carefully about what to do. Disaster is coming for our master and his whole household. He's so difficult that nobody can even talk to him.”
Abigail hurried and loaded donkeys with two hundred loaves, two containers of wine, five dressed sheep, five measures of roasted grain, a hundred clusters of raisins, and two hundred fig cakes.
She told her servants, “Go on ahead. I'll follow you.” She said nothing to her husband Nabal.
As she rode down along the hidden side of the mountain, David and his men came down toward her, and she met them.
David had been saying, “I guarded everything this man owned in the wilderness, and nothing of his went missing. It was all for nothing. He paid me back with evil for the good I did.
May God deal severely with David's enemies if I leave even one of Nabal's men alive by morning.”
As soon as Abigail saw David, she got off her donkey, fell facedown in front of him, and bowed to the ground.
At his feet she said, “My lord, let the blame fall on me. Please give me a chance to speak and hear what I have to say.
Please don't pay attention to that worthless man Nabal. He lives up to his name. His name means ‘fool,’ and foolishness follows him. I didn't see the young men you sent.

My lord, as surely as the LORD lives and as surely as you live, the LORD has kept you from bloodshed and from taking revenge with your own hands. May your enemies and everyone who wants to harm you end up like Nabal.
Please give this gift I've brought you to the young men who follow you.
Please forgive me. The LORD will establish a lasting family for you, my lord, because you fight his battles. May no wrongdoing be found in you all your life.
Even if someone comes after you to take your life, the LORD your God will keep you safe in the bundle of the living. He'll sling away the lives of your enemies like stones from a sling.
When the LORD has done all the good he promised you and made you ruler over Israel,
you won't have to live with the grief or guilt of shedding innocent blood or taking revenge yourself. When the LORD has been good to you, remember me.”
David told Abigail, “Praise the LORD, the God of Israel, who sent you to meet me today!
Bless you for your good judgment. You've kept me from bloodshed today and stopped me from taking revenge with my own hands.
As surely as the LORD, the God of Israel, lives, he kept me from harming you. If you hadn't come quickly to meet me, not one of Nabal's men would have been left alive by morning.”
David took the gift she'd brought and told her, “Go home in peace. I've listened to you and granted your request.”
When Abigail got home, Nabal was holding a feast fit for a king. He was in high spirits and very drunk, so she told him nothing until morning.
In the morning, after Nabal sobered up, Abigail told him what had happened. His heart failed him, and he became like a stone.
About ten days later the LORD struck Nabal, and he died.

When David heard Nabal was dead, he said, “Praise the LORD! He took up my case after Nabal insulted me and kept me from doing wrong. The LORD brought Nabal's wrongdoing back on his own head.” Then David sent word to Abigail asking her to marry him.
David's servants came to Abigail at Carmel and told her, “David sent us to bring you to him as his wife.”
She rose, bowed with her face to the ground, and said, “I'm ready to serve, even to wash the feet of my lord's servants.”
Abigail quickly got up and rode off on a donkey with her five attendants. She went with David's messengers and became his wife.
David had also married Ahinoam from Jezreel, so both women were his wives.
Saul had given his daughter Michal, David's wife, to Palti son of Laish, from Gallim.
The people of Ziph went to Saul at Gibeah and said, “Isn't David hiding on the hill of Hachilah, across from the desert?”
Saul went down into the wilderness of Ziph with three thousand chosen men of Israel to look for David there.
He camped beside the road on the hill of Hachilah across from the desert. David stayed in the wilderness and saw that Saul had come after him.
David sent scouts and found out for certain that Saul had arrived.
David went to Saul's camp and saw where Saul and his army commander Abner son of Ner were sleeping. Saul was inside the circle of wagons, with the troops camped around him.
David asked Ahimelech the Hittite and Abishai son of Zeruiah, Joab's brother, “Who'll go down to Saul's camp with me?” Abishai answered, “I'll go with you.”
David and Abishai reached the camp at night. Saul was asleep inside the circle of wagons, with his spear stuck in the ground near his head. Abner and the troops lay around him.
Abishai told David, “God has handed your enemy over to you today. Please let me kill him with his spear. One strike will be enough.”
David told him, “Don't kill him. Who can raise a hand against the LORD's anointed and stay innocent?”
David added, “As surely as the LORD lives, the LORD will strike him, or his time to die will come, or he'll go into battle and die there.
May the LORD keep me from raising my hand against his anointed. Take the spear and the water jar by his head, and let's go.”
David took the spear and water jar from beside Saul's head, and they left. Nobody saw them, knew what had happened, or woke up. The LORD had put everyone into a deep sleep.
David crossed over and stood on a hilltop far away, with plenty of distance between him and the camp.
He shouted to the troops and to Abner son of Ner, “Aren't you going to answer, Abner?” Abner answered, “Who are you, calling out to the king?”
David said, “Aren't you a capable man? Who in Israel is like you? Why didn't you guard your lord the king? Someone came into the camp to kill him.

You've failed at your duty. As surely as the LORD lives, you deserve to die because you didn't guard your lord, the LORD's anointed. Look for the king's spear and the water jar that were beside his head.”
Saul recognized David's voice and asked, “Is that you, my son David?” David answered, “It's me, my lord the king.”
He asked, “Why are you chasing your servant? What have I done? What evil am I guilty of?

Please hear me out, my lord the king. If the LORD has stirred you up against me, may he accept an offering. But if people have done it, may they be cursed before the LORD. They've driven me away from the LORD's inheritance, as if to say, ‘Go serve other gods.’
Don't let my blood fall far from the LORD's presence. The king of Israel has come out to hunt a flea, like someone hunting a partridge in the hills.”
Saul said, “I've sinned. Come back, my son David. I won't harm you again because you treated my life as precious today. I've acted like a fool and made a terrible mistake.”
David answered, “Here's your spear, King. Send one of your young men over to get it.
The LORD rewards each person for righteousness and faithfulness. He handed you over to me today, but I wouldn't raise my hand against his anointed.
Just as I valued your life today, may the LORD value mine and rescue me from all oppression.”
Saul told David, “May you be blessed, my son David. You'll do great things and you'll succeed.” David went on his way, and Saul went back home.
David thought, “One day Saul is going to kill me. My best chance is to escape to Philistine territory. Then Saul will give up looking for me in Israel, and I'll be out of his reach.”
So David crossed over with his six hundred men to Achish son of Maoch, king of Gath.
David and his men settled with Achish at Gath, each man with his household. David brought his two wives, Ahinoam from Jezreel and Abigail from Carmel, who had been Nabal's wife.
When Saul heard David had fled to Gath, he stopped looking for him.
David told Achish, “If I've found favor with you, let me have a place in one of the country towns. Why should your servant live with you in the royal city?”
Achish gave him Ziklag that day. That's why Ziklag has belonged to the kings of Judah ever since.
David lived in Philistine territory for a year and four months.
David and his men went up and raided the Geshurites, Girzites, and Amalekites. Those peoples had long lived in the land stretching toward Shur and as far as Egypt.
When David attacked, he left no man or woman alive. He took sheep, cattle, donkeys, camels, and clothing, then returned to Achish.
Achish asked, “Where did you raid today?” David told him, “The south of Judah, the south of the Jerahmeelites, and the south of the Kenites.”
David left no man or woman alive to bring back to Gath. He thought they might report what he had done. This was his practice the whole time he lived among the Philistines.
Achish trusted David. He thought, “David has made his own people Israel hate him. Now he'll serve me forever.”
Around that time the Philistines gathered their armies to fight Israel. Achish told David, “You and your men will be going out with me in the army.”
David answered, “Then you'll see what your servant can do.” Achish said, “Then I'll make you my bodyguard for life.”
Samuel had died, and all Israel had mourned him and buried him in his hometown of Ramah. Saul had driven the mediums and spiritists out of the land.
The Philistines gathered and camped at Shunem. Saul gathered all Israel, and they camped at Gilboa.
When Saul saw the Philistine army, he was terrified and his heart shook.
Saul asked the LORD for guidance, but the LORD didn't answer him through dreams, the Urim, or the prophets.
Saul told his servants, “Find me a woman who can speak with the dead so I can go and consult her.” His servants said, “There's a medium at Endor.”
Saul disguised himself in different clothes and went to the woman at night with two men. He asked, “Please consult a spirit for me and bring up whoever I name.”
She answered, “You know what Saul did. He drove out the mediums and spiritists. Why are you setting a trap to get me killed?”
Saul swore to her by the LORD, “As surely as the LORD lives, you won't be punished for this.”
She asked, “Who should I bring up for you?” He answered, “Bring up Samuel.”
When the woman saw Samuel, she screamed. She told Saul, “Why did you trick me? You're Saul!”
The king said, “Don't be afraid. What do you see?” She answered, “I see a god coming up out of the earth.”
He asked what he looked like. She said, “An old man is coming up, wrapped in a robe.” Saul realized it was Samuel and bowed with his face to the ground.

Samuel asked, “Why have you disturbed me by bringing me up?” Saul answered, “I'm in terrible trouble. The Philistines are fighting me and God has left me. He won't answer through prophets or dreams. So I've called you to tell me what to do.”
Samuel said, “Why are you asking me now that the LORD has left you and become your enemy?
The LORD has done just what he said through me. He's torn the kingdom out of your hands and given it to David, your neighbor.
You refused to listen to the LORD and didn't carry out his fierce anger against Amalek. That's why the LORD has done this to you today.
The LORD will hand Israel over to the Philistines along with you. Tomorrow you and your sons will be with me. The LORD will hand Israel's army over to the Philistines too.”
Saul immediately fell flat on the ground, terrified by Samuel's words. He had no strength left because he hadn't eaten anything all day and all night.
The woman came over and saw how distressed he was. She said, “I listened to you and risked my life by doing what you asked.
Now please listen to me. Let me give you something to eat so you have the strength to go on your way.”
Saul refused and said he wouldn't eat. But his servants and the woman kept urging him until he agreed. He got up from the ground and sat on the bed.
The woman had a fattened calf in the house. She quickly slaughtered it, then took flour, kneaded it, and baked bread without yeast.
She served the food to Saul and his servants, and they ate. Then they got up and left that night.
The Philistines gathered all their armies at Aphek, while the Israelites camped by the spring at Jezreel.
The Philistine rulers marched past with their troops in groups of hundreds and thousands. David and his men brought up the rear with Achish.

The Philistine commanders asked, “What are these Hebrews doing here?” Achish said, “This is David, who served King Saul of Israel. He's been with me for years. Since he came over to me, I haven't found any fault in him.”

But the commanders were angry. They told Achish, “Send him back to the place you gave him. He can't go into battle with us. He might turn against us in the fighting. What better way for him to win back his master's favor than with the heads of our men?
Isn't this the same David the women sang about as they danced? ‘Saul has killed his thousands, and David his tens of thousands.’”

Achish called David and told him, “As surely as the LORD lives, you've been honest with me. I've been glad to have you go out and come back with me in the army. From the day you came to me until now, I haven't found anything wrong with what you've done. But the other rulers don't trust you.
So turn back and go in peace. Don't do anything that would upset the Philistine rulers.”
David asked, “What have I done? What fault have you found in me since I entered your service? Why can't I go and fight the enemies of my lord the king?”
Achish answered, “As far as I'm concerned, you've been as good as an angel of God. But the Philistine commanders have said you can't go into battle with us.
Get up early tomorrow with the men who came with you from your master's service. Leave as soon as it's light.”
David and his men got up early and went back to Philistine territory, while the Philistines went up to Jezreel.
When David and his men reached Ziklag on the third day, they found the Amalekites had raided the south and attacked and burned Ziklag.
They had taken the women and everyone else captive, young and old. They hadn't killed anyone. They carried them off and went on their way.
David and his men found the city burned down, and their wives, sons, and daughters had been taken captive.
David and his men cried out and wept until they had no strength left to cry.
Both of David's wives had been taken captive: Ahinoam from Jezreel and Abigail from Carmel, Nabal's widow.
David was in deep distress. The men talked about stoning him because they were grieving for their sons and daughters. But David found strength in the LORD his God.
David told Abiathar the priest, Ahimelech's son, “Please bring me the ephod.” Abiathar brought it to him.
David asked the LORD, “If I go after these raiders, will I catch them?” The LORD answered, “Go after them. You'll catch them and recover everything.”
David set out with his six hundred men. They reached the Besor Brook, where some of the men stayed behind.
David kept going with four hundred men. The other two hundred were too exhausted to cross the brook and stayed there.
The men found an Egyptian in the field and brought him to David. They gave him bread to eat and water to drink.
They also gave him part of a fig cake and two clusters of raisins. After eating, he revived. He hadn't eaten or drunk anything for three days and three nights.
David asked, “Who do you belong to? Where are you from?” He answered, “I'm a young Egyptian, a servant of an Amalekite. My master left me when I got sick three days ago.
We raided the southern lands of the Cherethites, Judah, and Caleb, and burned Ziklag.”
David asked, “Will you take me to the raiders?” He answered, “Swear by God you won't kill me or hand me back to my master, and I'll take you to them.”
When the Egyptian led David there, the raiders were spread out across the ground, eating, drinking, and dancing over all the goods they'd taken from Philistine territory and Judah.
David fought them from twilight until the following evening. Only four hundred young men escaped, fleeing on camels.
David recovered everything the Amalekites had taken, including his two wives.
Nothing was missing, small or large, sons or daughters, goods or anything else the raiders had taken. David brought everything back.
David took all the flocks and herds. His men drove them ahead of their own livestock and said, “This is David's plunder.”
David came back to the two hundred men who'd been too exhausted to follow him and had stayed at the Besor Brook. They came out to meet David and his men, and David greeted them.
Some wicked men who'd gone with David said, “They didn't go with us, so they get none of the plunder we recovered. Each man can take his own wife and children and leave.”
David answered, “Don't do that, my brothers. The LORD gave us all this. He kept us safe and handed over the raiders who came against us.
Who would agree with you? The men who guard the supplies get the same share as the men who go into battle. They'll share equally.”
From that day forward David made it a law and rule for Israel, and it still stands today.
When David reached Ziklag, he sent some of the plunder to his friends among Judah's elders. “Here's a gift for you from what was taken from the LORD's enemies.”
He sent gifts to the people in Bethel, Ramoth in the south, and Jattir,
to the people in Aroer, Siphmoth, and Eshtemoa,
to the people in Racal and the towns of the Jerahmeelites and Kenites,
to those in Hormah, Borashan, and Athach,
and to Hebron and every other place where David and his men had stayed.
The Philistines fought Israel. The Israelites fled from them, and many were killed on Mount Gilboa.
The Philistines caught up with Saul and his sons and killed Jonathan, Abinadab, and Malchishua.
The battle closed in around Saul. The archers caught up with him, leaving him in great distress.
Saul asked his armor-bearer to kill him before the uncircumcised Philistines could kill and abuse him. His armor-bearer was too terrified to do it. So Saul took his own life with his sword.
When his armor-bearer saw that Saul was dead, he took his own life too and died beside him.
Saul, his three sons, his armor-bearer, and all his men died together that day.
When the Israelites across the valley and beyond the Jordan saw their army flee and learned that Saul and his sons were dead, they abandoned their towns and ran. The Philistines moved into the towns.
The next day the Philistines went to strip the bodies and found Saul and his three sons lying dead on Mount Gilboa.
They cut off Saul's head and took his armor. Then they sent the news throughout Philistine territory, to the temples of their idols and to the people.
They put his armor in the temple of the Ashtaroth and fastened his body to the wall of Beth Shan.
The people of Jabesh Gilead heard what the Philistines had done to Saul.
All their brave men traveled through the night and took the bodies of Saul and his sons down from the wall of Beth Shan. They brought them to Jabesh and burned them there.
They buried their bones under the tamarisk tree at Jabesh and fasted for seven days.
